label: paragraph_title
text: "DRASTIC ECONOMY" ESTIMATES.

label: text
text: Last year the most arresting feature of the Governor's budget speech in the Legislative Council was not so much the exceptionally heavy programme of public works outlined for 1925—over $9,000,000 was set aside for public works extraordinary alone—nor yet the many improvements promised for the various Government departments in the way of increased staffs and better facilities: the most arresting feature of the budget speech last year was the financial policy His Excellency advocated, not merely for 1925, but for the much longer period implied by the words "near future." Briefly this policy was to press forward development works with every speed, even if this entailed a deficit for the year, each year, the deficit to be met from our cash balances, care being taken, of course, not to deplete these beyond a point—His Excellenceary suggested $5,000,000—where any sudden call would dislocate our finances. Once our cash balances had been thus reduced, the time would have come to seek elsewhere for the money with which to finance certain desfrable.

label: text
text: when completed, pay for themselves and possibly yield a profit; long term loans for development works which would not bring any appreciable return but which would prove of equal, if not of greater value to future generations. This policy naturally commended itself greatly to the public, since the Governor was able to promise that under it, for many years, to come, materially increased taxation could be avoided, even if the revenue from opium should cease to figure in our returns.

label: text
text: That was the outlook this time last year.

label: text
text:
How different it is to-day as a result of the strike and boycott can be seen from the budget speech Sir Edward Stubbs delivered in the Legislative Council this afternoon. An estimate of revenue is necessarily at any time a rather uncertain thing, he observed, being at best an expression of belief or an aspiration, but in the present case he could not claim that it was anything more than a guess—“whether a good guess or a bad one we cannot hope to tell until long after I have left the Colony.” Instead of speeding up development work as planned in the last budget, the Government is now making “every possible effort to effect economies,” and while “cannot hope to close the year without a heavy deficit,” it is comforting to note that “in any case our balances are sufficient to cover any possible deficit this year and to leave us a margin which should enable us to carry on through the year 1926 without imposing additional burdens on the taxpayer unless the situation should become materially worse than it is at present.”
What are the prospects of the situation becoming materially worse?
Next to the immediate financial question, involving as it did possible further taxation that question represents the most important side of the budget speech. How long does the Government from its special vantage point consider the trouble will last?

label: text
text: spect of the Colony's revenue already shows signs of improvement, and relying on the intelligence of the people of Kwangtung, "a race famous for centuries for its commercial ability and practical sense," to throw off the present oppressive régime in Canton, Sir Edward Stubbs thinks it is being not over sanguine to hope for the establishment of good order by the end of this year or early in the next. None the less he feels that, looking to the harm already done and the vast losses to South China, "it must be years before the consequences cease to be felt." That, we think, represents the considered views of most sensible people here, and it is distinctly reassuring to find the Government so alert to the needs of the new situation, for such confidence will be one of the chief factors in the weathering of our present troubles. Sir Edward Stubbs deserves the Colony's thanks for the courage and foresight he has again shown in this the last, but by no means the least, of the budgets he has framed for Hongkong.

label: text
text: PICKETB AGAIN ACTIVM.

label: text
text:
Ten strikers from each union in Canton have been asked to volunteer for cooling service with the Red troops on the East River front, states a report from Canton.
When the military wanted transport men they approached the Strike Executive. The latter called a meeting and it was decided to call for volunteers. The pay per month, per man, is said to be $18.

label: text
text: Tau, the Chinese district near Deep Bay—beyond the New Territory. A batch of new men, numbering about 200, have replaced the old strikers. The Canton obsolete gunboat "Po Pik" is anchored in the vicinity and an armed launch is cruising near the place where the ferry leaves for Hongkong. Passengers are not allowed to depart and food export is prohibited but a small quantity gets through occasionally.

label: text
text: Three Canton warships, the "Kong Kung," "Kwong On," and the "Ping Nam" are reported to have gone to Chinshan to assist the strike pickets.

label: paragraph_title
text: MISCHA LEVITZKI.

label: text
text: FINAL RECITAL HERE TO-NIGHT.

label: text
text: TRIBUTE OF A CRITIO.

label: text
text: Hongkong has already had opportunity to take measure of the artistic stature of Mischi Levitzki and will have another and last opportunity to do so to night, when Mr. Levitzki will give his final recital at the Theatre Royal. It is interesting to quote the critic of the "Chicago Post" on the occasion of Levitzki's recent appearance in that city. He wrote as follows: Levitzki is one of those intended by nature to play the piano. Everything he does is conceived in terms of the piano and in his wide ranging he is never tempted to transgress its bounds. There were moments of exquisite beauty in the Chopin-lovely tone colours with the inner voices weaving their melodies together in happy adjustment and with the pianistic sense governing all. It was the forefell Chopin with the man's brain back of the post's eye. At to night's recital Mr. Levitzki will again present a group entirely devoted to the works of Chopin including the military Polanais. To hear Levitzki play Chopin is a treat no music lover can afford to miss.

FREEDOM OF SPEECH.
Hongkong, October 8,
THE REGISTERED LETTER PROBLEM.
(To the Editor of the China Mail).
Sir, — We acknowledge that the Post Office is responsible for the safe delivery of registered letters, and that, in the interests of the receivers were such precautions taken, as have been adopted, for some time past, and are being still adopted.
Where, however, registered articles can be conveniently delivered, directly or indirectly to the addresses without any chances of miscarriage or loss. I am sure that a suggestion in which safety is not sacrificed for convenience, will receive due considerations.
Registered letters from overseas addressed to Chinese undergrudines of Hongkong University might in these unsettled times safely be sent up to the Registrar's office, instead of presenting a siderable inconvenience to the addresses by asking these letters to be called for as has hitherto been the case.
